text: We introduce GR00T 2, a new generation of foundation world-action models (WAMs) . GR00T 2 predicts future video and robot actions together, learning how physical interactions unfold along with the actions that produce them. The models run on parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoids. Learning to predict the world, not just act in it, unlocks three new capabilities. Skills shown only by humans, or with handheld and wearable devices, carry over to robots that never practiced them. GR00T 2 performs many new tasks zero-shot and masters them from a handful of demonstrations. Because it predicts the outcome it is acting toward, a reasoning model can also direct it. GR00T 2 Turbo is GR00T 2 built for speed. A smaller transformer and a more compact video representation make it light enough to run on the Unitree G1 humanoid itself, steering the robot's whole body as it walks, bends, reaches, and carries. One diffusion transformer denoises future video and robot actions together. Predicting how the scene should change lets GR00T 2 learn physics from human video; small per-robot heads turn the plan into motor commands for each body. GR00T 2 reads recent video, the instruction and the robot state, denoises future video and an action chunk together, executes the chunk, and repeats. GR00T 2 is pretrained on one mixture of three kinds of data: 402,730 hours of egocentric video of people at work, 10,184 hours of demonstrations with a handheld UMI gripper across 2,897 tasks, and 23,500 hours of robot teleoperation. The robot data spans parallel-gripper arms (YAM and Franka), dexterous hands (Sharpa and Wuji), and the Unitree G1 humanoid. The human video comes from our egocentric Human-1M dataset, and 100,000 hours of it are openly available as Human-1M-100K on Hugging Face, which you can browse in the Human-1M Dataset Explorer . Human video is by far the largest part of the mixture. To measure how much it helps the robot as it scales, we pretrain four models on none, 1%, 10%, and 100% of the human video, then evaluate each on 72 downstream Dexter tasks, both as video rollouts and on the real robot. GEAR DexUMI is a wearable exoskeleton that matches a robot hand's joints, so what a person does with it maps directly onto the robot. From DexUMI demonstrations alone, GR00T 2 learns three bimanual tasks on a Tianji robot with two XHAND1 hands: preparing banana yogurt and scooping granola, the two halves of a breakfast task, and striking a match to light a lamp under a flask before putting the match out in water. Post-trained for about six epochs on a small dataset per task, GR00T 2 learns each task from a few hours of demonstrations. GR00T 2 is pretrained on teleoperation data from many robots and on large-scale human video, and it learns by predicting how the world changes as it acts. Because it has seen so many tasks, a skill shown on one embodiment, or only in human video, carries over to a robot that has never practiced it. We test this on 50 tasks that appear in other robots' data or in human video but never in the target robot's own data: a bimanual robot with two Sharpa hands. Zero-shot, from the instruction alone, GR00T 2 succeeds in 40% of trials, and on 40 of the 50 tasks it succeeds at least once. Most misses come from execution, not intent: GR00T 2 does the right steps in the right order, and a single step falls short on precision. A little robot data closes that gap. One demonstration per task lifts success to 71%, and five, under 3 minutes of robot data , lift it to 95%, with 37 of the 50 tasks succeeding in every trial. Each adaptation is a 30-minute LoRA fine-tune on a single RTX 5090 . Zero-shot runs the pretrained model as is; 1-shot and 5-shot fine-tune it with LoRA on 1 or 5 demonstrations per task. Six long-horizon assembly and insertion tasks on YAM, each post-trained for about six epochs. 20 trials per task and model. Reinforcement learning on the real robot, driven only by task-level success signals, lifts all three contact-rich tasks: from 40–76% success after supervised post-training to 88–96% with GRPO-induced self-imitation. A frontier reasoning agent and GR00T 2 handle complementary parts of a task. The agent decides what to do: it breaks a long task into steps, checks progress, and writes code. GR00T 2 decides how , performing the contact-rich manipulation that is hard to script. Through the WAM API, the agent can control GR00T 2 as a tool and steer it by marking targets on its camera view. The agent runs as System 2 (S2). In an observe–reason–act–verify loop, it calls GR00T 2 as a tool alongside tools for camera images, robot state, and code-as-policy (CaP) skills. On real robots, GR00T 2 performs most of the manipulation. The agent watches it, and when a part drops or progress stalls, it repairs the scene with a CaP skill learned with ASPIRE and hands control back. In simulation, the agent instead runs a task-level program that calls GR00T 2 for each manipulation step. We also used simulation to develop recovery skills for some assembly tasks and then transferred them to the real robot. Each assembly trial starts by dumping all parts onto the table, so every trial begins from a cluttered layout that does not appear in the post-training data. With the agent, GR00T 2 assembles the toy plane, the toy tractor, and the Hot Wheels car in 98, 97, and 97 of 100 trials. With visual steering, the planner marks a grasp point on the target object and a release point at its destination on GR00T 2's camera view, colored by the arm that should act. GR00T 2 generates the rest of the motion: approach, grasp, transport, and release. After each step, the planner looks again and decides whether to continue, retry, or stop. Training needs no new data: the marks are extracted from the gripper and hand states in existing demonstrations, and the same model still follows language alone. Both robots are evaluated with the same protocol, in three settings: GR00T 2 given only the task instruction, the planner's step instructions, or the step instructions together with marks. On short-horizon instructions about what to move and where, visual steering (step instructions plus marks) raises success from 40% to 92% on YAM and from 30% to 70% on Dexter, whereas the planner's step instructions alone reach 66% and 33%. On instructions about how to move, such as the action type or the grasp type, the gain is smaller: 44% to 59% on YAM. YAM: 90 what-and-where and 54 how trials per setting. Dexter: 64 trials per setting, all what-and-where. Over long horizons, these single-step gains compound. On YAM, GR00T 2 without marks completes no trash-sorting or board-disassembly episode, even with the planner's step instructions; with marks, it completes 17 of 20 and 3 of 10. On Dexter, the marks place more items in trash sorting but rarely complete the full task, which is the current limit of the system. Marks also convey neither an object's final orientation nor the motion between grasp and release, such as pouring or wiping; those still come from language. 20 trash-sorting and 10 NIST board-disassembly episodes per setting. A humanoid must place its hands precisely while staying balanced as its whole body moves, often quickly. With its lower prediction cost, GR00T 2 Turbo runs onboard a Unitree G1 and steers the SONIC whole-body controller through latent whole-body commands. The videos below show it serving and delivering popcorn, cleaning up a spill, and picking up trash in an office cafeteria. GR00T 2 Turbo lowers the cost of world-action modeling in two ways: a smaller joint video–action transformer (2B parameters) and a higher-compression video encoder that exploits redundancy in video. It still predicts future observations and actions jointly, with the same action horizon, and it is the model behind the onboard G1 results below. Turbo also remains competitive on other embodiments. On YAM it reaches 90% on fixed-pipe fittings and 100% on inserting a wire into a breaker, ahead of GR00T 2 on both. It trails GR00T 2 on the other four YAM tasks and on five of the six Dexter tasks in the post-training charts above, tying on the sixth. The Dexterity and YAM post-training charts report both variants task by task. Turbo's smaller transformer and compact video representation, together with inference optimizations shared by every configuration below, make onboard execution possible. The optimizations cut median prediction latency by 66–86% (2.9–7.2×) relative to eager BF16 execution of the same checkpoint. Optimized, a Turbo prediction for G1 takes 38 ms on an RTX 5090 and 124 ms onboard Jetson Thor, where it plans 1.6 s chunks of whole-body motion tokens about once per second; SONIC executes them at 50 Hz. Eager BF16 → optimized. A reasoning model chooses the task; GR00T 2 Turbo imagines and plans; SONIC turns latent whole-body tokens into joint targets. Everything but the reasoning model runs onboard. Scooping and serving popcorn, cleaning up a spill, and clearing a table of diverse objects, all on the same humanoid: bimanual tool use, whole-body reach, and long-horizon clean-up. 48 trials for popcorn, 30 for each other task. With simulated data added, GR00T 2 Turbo's out-of-distribution success rises from 6.7% to 63.3%. GR00T 1.7 rises to 40.0%. Same real data; one arm adds simulated episodes. We developed an agentic real-to-sim workflow that recreates high-fidelity digital twins of real-world tasks and use these simulation environments for policy evaluation and development. The task set spans rigid and articulated objects, deformable materials, high-precision assembly, and particles with diverse interactions including, but not limited to, sliding, pushing and scooping. Agent-assisted workflows build the environments. Agents take inputs such as real robot videos, 3D scans, and photographs and use tools from SimFoundry to reconstruct the scene and assets, including geometry, appearance, and collision modeling. Reconstructed environments are validated through a combination of automated tests (replaying existing demonstrations and stability tests) and human expert feedback given to the agent for refinement. Policy evaluations in these high-fidelity digital twins proved to have strong correlations with real-world evaluations, allowing them to accelerate GR00T 2 development. Changes to the data loading and processing pipeline were tested with small-scale training and closed-loop simulation before adoption in pretraining. Inference settings were screened in simulation before robot tests.
